summary.text: For \(n=9\), the value is \(223092870^2+1=49770428644836901=29^2\cdot59180057841661\). Thus it has the squared prime divisor \(29^2\) and is not squarefree, so the conjunction fails regardless of the infinitude claim.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p_0=2,p_1=3,p_2=5,\ldots\) denote the primes in increasing order, and define the \(n\)-th primorial in the indexing used here by
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}p_k,
\]
with the empty product \(P_0=1\). Thus the sequence is
\[
a(n)=P_n^2+1.
\]
The conjecture is the conjunction of the following two assertions:

1. \(a(n)\) is squarefree for every nonnegative integer \(n\);
2. the set of \(n\) for which \(a(n)\) is prime is infinite.

It suffices to disprove the first assertion, since a conjunction is false whenever either one of its conjuncts is false.

Consider the term with index \(n=9\). The first nine primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23.
\]
Their product can be evaluated successively as
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\cdot3&=6,\\
6\cdot5&=30,\\
30\cdot7&=210,\\
210\cdot11&=2310,\\
2310\cdot13&=30030,\\
30030\cdot17&=510510,\\
510510\cdot19&=9699690,\\
9699690\cdot23&=223092870.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
P_9=223092870
\]
and hence
\[
a(9)=223092870^2+1=49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901.
\]

We now show that this number has a nontrivial square divisor. Modulo \(29^2=841\), the primorial has the decomposition
\[
223092870=841\cdot265270+800.
\]
Since \(800\equiv-41\pmod{841}\), it follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(9)
  &=223092870^2+1\\
  &\equiv(-41)^2+1\\
  &=1681+1\\
  &=1682\\
  &=2\cdot841
  \equiv0\pmod{841}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(841=29^2\) divides \(a(9)\). The exact division is
\[
49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901
 =841\cdot59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661.
\]
Equivalently, one may display the factorization
\[
a(9)=29^2\cdot53\cdot1{,}116{,}604{,}864{,}937,
\]
since
\[
53\cdot1{,}116{,}604{,}864{,}937
=59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661.
\]

A positive integer is squarefree precisely when no square \(d^2\) with \(d>1\) divides it; equivalently, no square of a prime divides it. Here \(29>1\) and \(29^2\mid a(9)\), so \(a(9)\) is not squarefree. If one uses the prime-square formulation directly, note that \(29\) is prime: any proper prime divisor would be at most \(\sqrt{29}<6\), while \(29\) is divisible by none of \(2,3,5\).

Therefore the universal claim that every \(a(n)\) is squarefree already fails at \(n=9\). Hence the conjunction
\[
\bigl(\forall n,\ a(n)\text{ is squarefree}\bigr)
\quad\land\quad
\bigl(\text{infinitely many }n\text{ have }a(n)\text{ prime}\bigr)
\]
is false, independently of whether the second, infinitude assertion is true or false. This disproves the stated conjecture.
